article_title: The Effects of Charter High Schools on Educational Attainment
citation: Kevin Booker, Tim R. Sass, Brian Gill, Ron Zimmer. (2011). The Effects of Charter High Schools on Educational Attainment. Journal of Labor Economics, vol. 29, no. 2. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Consider charter high school continuity when designing middle-to-high-school transition supports for charter middle school students
description: The article's findings suggest that where students enroll after charter middle school is consequential for attainment: continuing into a charter high school was associated with higher diploma earning and college attendance than "transitioned to a traditional public high school". School systems and families weighing high school options for charter middle school graduates may treat high school sector continuity as a relevant consideration, alongside the study's Florida and Chicago scope.
requirements: Applies to students who attended a charter middle school and are choosing between charter and traditional public high schools.
constraints: Evidence is limited to Florida and Chicago as analyzed in this study.
target_learners: Charter middle school students transitioning to high school
target_learning_goals: High school diploma attainment
College attendance
examples: The study compared charter middle school graduates who continued into charter high schools with those who entered traditional public high schools in Florida and Chicago.
key_sources: Kevin Booker, Tim R. Sass, Brian Gill, Ron Zimmer. (2011). The Effects of Charter High Schools on Educational Attainment. Journal of Labor Economics, vol. 29, no. 2. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/the-effects-of-charter-high-schools-on-educational-attainment

article_title: Survey of Outcomes Measurement in Research on Character Education Programs
citation: Person, Ann E., Emily Moiduddin, Megan Hague-Angus, and Lizabeth M. Malone (2009). Survey of Outcomes Measurement in Research on Character Education Programs (NCEE 2009-006). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ncee.ed.gov
title: Character education evaluators should ground measure selection in a theory of change or work backward from an outcome taxonomy, and choose measures with demonstrated reliability and validity
description: The report recommends that researchers selecting outcome measures for character education evaluations first reference "a clear theory of how program elements are linked to specific out comes" to identify the constructs a program is most likely to affect; in the absence of such a theory, they can "work backward" from the report's taxonomy to select appropriate constructs. It further advises selecting or developing measures with demonstrated reliability and validity, given the complexity of character as a construct, and calls for more consistent reporting of psychometric properties across studies.
requirements: Access to the report's outcome taxonomy and its crosswalk of measures with reported reliability of .70 or greater
constraints: The measures presented are not necessarily representative of the universe of character education research nor necessarily the best measures available; the report provides no guidance on or recommendations of specific measures
target_learners: K-12 students in character education programs, including PCEP grantees
target_learning_goals: character development outcomes across cognitive, affective, and behavioral domains
examples: The report highlights misalignment risks it observed: scale items that do not hang together, and mismatches between the construct a measure actually captures and the construct the researcher reports
key_sources: Person, Ann E., Emily Moiduddin, Megan Hague-Angus, and Lizabeth M. Malone (2009). Survey of Outcomes Measurement in Research on Character Education Programs (NCEE 2009-006). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/survey-of-outcomes-measurement-in-research-on-character-education-programs

article_title: Changing Standards, Changing Relationships
citation: Roderick, M., Stone, S., with Arney, M., Chiong, J., DaCosta, K., & Waxman, E. (1998). Changing Standards, Changing Relationships: Building Family-School Relationships to Promote Achievement in High Schools. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://ccsr.uchicago.edu/publications/changing-standards-changing-relationships-building-family-school-relationships-promote
title: Increasing parental involvement in high schools requires changing teachers' and schools' outreach practices, not just expecting parents to engage
description: The brief argues that raising parental involvement at the high school level must begin with changes in what high schools and teachers do: communicating about academic goals, giving parents direction for supporting learning, and making schools more inviting. It finds that "High schools have discouraged parent involvement by being less inviting to parents and by making it harder for parents to get information and resources." Schools that improved instruction also improved parent relationships, supporting a dual-focus approach.
requirements: High school teachers and administrators must see working with parents as part of their role
constraints: High schools face structural barriers including larger workloads, fewer informal contact opportunities, and in Hispanic-serving schools, language barriers and overcrowding
target_learners: high school students, particularly ninth graders
target_learning_goals: academic achievement through increased home support and monitoring of schoolwork
examples: Fenger High School adopted family math nights, parent orientations, a parent advisory council, a paid parent aide, and informal family social nights to open communication and build parent skills
Roosevelt High School's Parent Center combined monthly workshops in Spanish and English, volunteer coordination, and individualized family counseling services

Changing Standards, Changing Relationships: Building Family-School Relationships to Promote Achievement in High Schools. article_title: Equity in the Driver’s Seat: A Practice-Driven, Equity-Centered Approach for Setting R&D Agendas in Education
citation: Babe Liberman and Viki Young, Ph.D. (2020). Equity in the Driver's Seat: A Practice-Driven, Equity-Centered Approach for Setting R&D Agendas in Education. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Select challenge topics that have an existing research base, remaining gaps, and timeliness in policy and equity conversations
description: The article recommends three criteria for selecting challenge topics for practice-driven R&D agenda-setting: a strong existing body of field knowledge with remaining research gaps, being a hot topic in policy, practice, and equity, and an ongoing need for research synthesis, solution development, or technical assistance. 'Appropriate challenge topics have a research base to start from, but are not fully developed, with meaningful gaps in the research that can be filled based on practice perspectives.' Adolescent literacy and computational thinking were selected because both met these criteria.
requirements: Topics must be relevant and urgent to both the research and practice sides
target_learners: Adolescents behind in reading proficiency and K-12 students in computational learning opportunities
target_learning_goals: Focusing R&D investment on persistent, equity-relevant challenges where practice perspectives can fill research gaps
examples: Adolescent literacy was chosen because less is known about supporting adolescents severely behind in reading, and CT because best practices for implementing CT competencies across grade levels remain unclear

article_title: Policies and Practices That Meet Learners Where They Are
citation: Barbara Pape and Tom Vander Ark. (2020). Policies and Practices That Meet Learners Where They Are. Digital Promise Global. https://global.digitalpromise.org
title: Challenge Based Learning framework: three phases with key design elements
description: The paper describes Challenge Based Learning as connecting student projects to real-world challenges, divided into three interconnected phases: Engage, Investigate, and Act. It lists key elements including that everyone is a learner, learning moves beyond the classroom walls, challenges are learner-inspired and owned, there is space and freedom to fail, technology is authentically used, and learners continuously reflect. As printed: "The CBL Framework is divided into three interconnected phases – Engage, Investigate, and Act."
requirements: Community involvement beyond the classroom; ubiquitous access to information and technology; intentional slowing for critical and creative thinking; documentation and reflection throughout
constraints: Described as a framework with design elements; the paper reports no comparative effectiveness data for it
target_learners: K-12 students working on collaborative real-world challenges with teachers, families, and community members
target_learning_goals: Deep subject area knowledge and skills for thriving in an ever-changing world, including collaboration and creative problem solving
examples: The framework's elements include a safe space to fail, receive feedback and try again, with iteration built into all phases
key_sources: Barbara Pape and Tom Vander Ark. (2020). Policies and Practices That Meet Learners Where They Are. Digital Promise Global. https://global.digitalpromise.org

article_title: Small Schools on a Larger Scale
citation: Kahne, J. E., Sporte, S., de la Torre, M., with Easton, J. Q. (2006). Small High Schools on a Larger Scale: The First Three Years of the Chicago High School Redesign Initiative. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/small-high-schools-larger-scale
title: CHSRI small schools theory of action
description: The report maps the Chicago High School Redesign Initiative's theory of action: district resources and policies create small voluntary schools with limited bureaucratic regulation, which foster a teacher context of "trust, collective responsibility, and teacher influence"; this context supports instructional-improvement activities leading to higher-quality instruction, while smaller personal environments plus shared curricular themes are expected to raise expectations and academic and personal support for students, ultimately improving outcomes. The report quantitatively tests Boxes 6 through 10 of this framework.
requirements: Appropriate district resources and policies to create the small schools
Balancing small school autonomy and flexibility with accountability and support from CHSRI staff and the district
constraints: The report examined only the theory elements assessable quantitatively (Boxes 6-10); qualitative work covered Boxes 1-5 but is not detailed in this report
target_learners: Low-income students of color in large urban public high schools, particularly Chicago ninth- and eleventh-graders
target_learning_goals: Improved attendance, on-track status, dropout prevention, and achievement test performance through supportive school contexts and instructional improvement
examples: The initiative converted three large underperforming high schools into twelve autonomous small schools between 2002 and 2004, sharing buildings but not administrative staff or discretionary funds
key_sources: Kahne, J. E., Sporte, S., de la Torre, M., with Easton, J. Q. (2006). Small High Schools on a Larger Scale: The First Three Years of the Chicago High School Redesign Initiative. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/small-schools-larger-scale-first-three-years-chicago-high-school-redesign-initiative

article_title: School Improvement with External Partners
citation: Fred M. Newmann, Karin Sconzert. (2000). School Improvement with External Partners. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://ccsr.uchicago.edu/sites/default/files/publications/ExternalPartners.pdf
title: Chicago Annenberg External Partner model for school improvement
description: The external partner model links intermediary organizations (university- or community-based) to networks of schools to provide outside expertise for improvement efforts. Partners sponsor activities including network meetings, instructional materials, school-based literacy coordinators, demonstration teachers, leadership teams, and parent assistants. The model emerged from Chicago's decentralization movement and the 1995 Annenberg Challenge, which provided $49.2 million to fund 45 networks of schools with external partners focused on goals such as improving literacy instruction and developing school leadership.
requirements: Requires networks of three or more schools with a committed external partner relationship
Partners must be voluntarily selected by schools
constraints: Partner involvement occupies only a minor part of schools' attention, limiting influence
Initial budget requirements limited external partners to only 10 percent of any total grant made to a network
target_learners: K-12 students in urban public schools
target_learning_goals: Whole-school change in instruction, leadership, professional community, parent involvement, and learning climate
examples: Nine Chicago Annenberg partners studied from 1996-1999, including five university-based, two community-based, one community advocacy, and one cultural institution partner
key_sources: Fred M. Newmann, Karin Sconzert. (2000). School Improvement with External Partners. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://ccsr.uchicago.edu/sites/default/files/publications/ExternalPartners.pdf

article_title: Project Cal-Well: Building Sustainable School-Based Mental Health Systems
citation: Project Cal-Well: Building Sustainable School-Based Mental Health Systems. (2024). WestEd. https://wested.org
title: CHKS Mental Health Supports module and companion School Staff Survey Student Wellness Module
description: For the comprehensive Project Cal-Well evaluation, UCSF "created a custom Mental Health Supports module for the California Healthy Kids Survey (CHKS)" to assess changes in students' mental health needs and access to support. In partnership with WestEd the module was expanded with trauma measures and is now part of the CHKS Behavioral Health Modules available to LEAs statewide. UCSF also developed a companion Student Wellness Module of the School Staff Survey to assess staff capacity to support student mental health over time.
requirements: Administered through the California Healthy Kids Survey system so LEAs statewide can use the behavioral health modules
constraints: Developed as part of the Project Cal-Well evaluation under the SAMHSA-funded grant
target_learners: K-12 students and school staff in California local educational agencies
target_learning_goals: Assessing student mental health needs, access to support, trauma exposure, and staff capacity to support student mental health
examples: The module was expanded to include additional measures on trauma and is now part of the CHKS Behavioral Health Modules available to LEAs statewide

article_title: Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools, Part 1: The Role and Perspective of Charter School Authorizers
citation: National Charter School Resource Center, lead authors Aimee Evan, Laura Groth, and Hannah Sullivan. (2020). Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools: Part 1 The Role and Perspective of Charter School Authorizers. Bethesda, MD: Manhattan Strategy Group. https://ncsrc.org
title: Taxonomy of indicators of distress and indicators of failure in charter schools
description: The report distinguishes leading 'indicators of distress' — characteristics occurring early in a school's decline that 'tend to be more difficult to measure and easier to influence than lagging indicators' — from lagging 'indicators of failure,' output data points occurring later that are easier to measure but 'require more substantive interventions to influence.' Distress indicators are organized into seven categories: leadership, governing board, operations, finance, talent, culture, and instruction, derived from a literature review and authorizer perspectives, and categorized using the Four Domains for Rapid School Improvement framework adapted to the charter context.
requirements: Indicators must be locally validated in each authorizing context before use as predictors of distress
constraints: Not all indicators will show up in each struggling school; authorizers' capacity and policy directives limit which indicators they can collect and examine
target_learners: Charter school authorizers and state education agencies
target_learning_goals: Identifying struggling charter schools early enough for manageable intervention
examples: Table 1 lists distress indicators such as mismatched leadership competencies, inability to convene the board, breakdown in compliance, and failure to properly manage finances, alongside failure indicators such as declines in achievement, growth, graduation rates, and financial viability
key_sources: National Charter School Resource Center, lead authors Aimee Evan, Laura Groth, and Hannah Sullivan. (2020). Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools: Part 1 The Role and Perspective of Charter School Authorizers. Bethesda, MD: Manhattan Strategy Group. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED609911

article_title: Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools, Part 2: The Roles and Perspectives of Charter School Leaders and Board Members
citation: National Charter School Resource Center, Evan, A., & Sullivan, H. (2021). Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools, Part 2: The Roles and Perspectives of Charter School Leaders and Board Members. Bethesda, MD: Manhattan Strategy Group.
title: Charter ecosystem model: external stakeholders and environmental shifts as sources of and buffers against school distress
description: The report's second finding holds that school decline is systematic and partly external: "a charter schools' context—or ecosystem—can also be a source of challenges." The ecosystem model maps the school at the center of parents/community, district, network, authorizer, and state actors that shape its environment (Figure 3). "Being aware of these external stressors helped schools prevent a challenge from occurring," and ecosystems "can aid or impede a charter school's ability to overcome stressors," so schools should scan their context to anticipate shifts and prevent decline.
requirements: Ongoing awareness of the operating context so schools can prepare for and remediate potential challenges before they occur
constraints: Some circumstances, such as the COVID pandemic, arise suddenly and cannot be anticipated; the report's evidence comes from schools that had already experienced distress
target_learners: Charter school leaders and boards
Authorizers, districts, networks, and state policymakers in the ecosystem
target_learning_goals: Preventing organizational decline by anticipating environmental shifts affecting the school's learning conditions
examples: Figure 3 diagrams the charter ecosystem with school, parents/community, district, network, authorizer, and state as key actors
key_sources: National Charter School Resource Center, Evan, A., & Sullivan, H. (2021). Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools, Part 2: The Roles and Perspectives of Charter School Leaders and Board Members. Bethesda, MD: Manhattan Strategy Group. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED616211

article_title: The Tapestry of American Public Education: How Can We Create a System of Schools Worth Choosing for All?
citation: Cookson, P. W., Jr., Darling-Hammond, L., Rothman, R., & Shields, P. M. (2018). The tapestry of American public education: How we can create a system of schools worth choosing for all? Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/tapestry-american-public-education
title: Choice systems improve quality only when paired with instructional improvement strategies that build capacity in all schools
description: The report argues that choice alone does not raise quality: "Simply creating new options does not lead automatically to greater access, quality, or equity." Districts that paired choice with intensive, content-based professional development, classroom walkthroughs with rubrics, and curricular support (NYC District 2, Milwaukee) saw achievement gains, while New Orleans, where central support was cut, produced an uneven set of schools. The principle directs policymakers to invest in teaching capacity across all schools rather than relying on choice dynamics alone.
requirements: A strong infrastructure of professional development and financial and curricular resources so all students have access to strong schools
constraints: Without a support system to help schools improve, the only recourse for school failure is closure, leaving students moving from one failing school to another
target_learners: All public school students in choice systems
target_learning_goals: Access to high-quality teaching and curricula in every school
examples: NYC District 2 built professional development and resources so all schools became higher quality; Milwaukee's gains began only after an instructional improvement initiative for district-run schools
key_sources: Cookson, P. W., Jr., Darling-Hammond, L., Rothman, R., & Shields, P. M. (2018). The tapestry of American public education: How we can create a system of schools worth choosing for all? article_title: 5 Things for Advocates to Know about Chronic Absenteeism
citation: EdTrust. (2023). 5 Things for Advocates to Know About Chronic Absenteeism. https://EdTrust.org
title: Chronic absence is a reflection of the school and community environment, so improve conditions for learning
description: This principle frames chronic absence as an indicator of systemic conditions rather than individual failing. The brief states "Chronic absence reflects the challenges students face in school, such as bullying, lack of an engaging curriculum or meaningful relationships, and feeling physically or emotionally unsafe." It also results from insufficient community resources like unstable housing, inadequate healthcare, and poor transportation. High absence levels reflect systemic challenges and historical discrimination requiring programmatic or policy solutions.
requirements: Policymakers and practitioners creating environments where students and families feel welcome and valued
Professional development helping adults build relationships and support students from diverse backgrounds
constraints: Barriers are cyclical: lack of meaningful relationships leads to disengagement and absence, which then prevents building belonging
target_learners: K-12 students affected by adverse school or community conditions
target_learning_goals: Engagement in school
Positive, equitable learning conditions
examples: The brief urges leaders to use school climate data for improvement, ensure curriculum is rigorous and reflective of students' diverse experiences, and use chronic absence data to allocate resources where disparities are greatest.
key_sources: EdTrust. (2023). 5 Things for Advocates to Know About Chronic Absenteeism. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED627994

article_title: The AI disruption in engineering education: an analysis of changing student norms through cultural historical activity
citation: Tiina Leino Lindell, Christian Stöhr. (2026). The AI disruption in engineering education: an analysis of changing student norms through cultural historical activity theory. Journal of Computing in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12528-025-09488-8
title: Cultural-Historical Activity Theory as a framework for analyzing how GenAI transforms educational activity systems
description: The study adopts Cultural-Historical Activity Theory (CHAT) as its analytical framework, understanding human action as mediated by tools within an activity system of six interconnected components: rules, tools, subjects, division of labor, community, and object. In CHAT, norms are "implicit rules that regulate activity", and contradictions are historically and culturally situated tensions that arise when new elements such as GenAI disrupt established practices. The article treats these contradictions not as obstacles but as "the driving force of change in activity", using them as analytical entry points to explain how students' GenAI use transforms norms and practices in engineering education.
requirements: Analysis requires identifying contradictions as tensions between components of the activity system, following the recommendations of Sannino and Engeström (2018) and Virtaluoto et al. (2016) as the article states
constraints: The authors call their introduction to CHAT "short and necessary incomplete"
The framework was applied to one technical university in Northern Europe, so the analysis is context-sensitive to that setting
target_learners: Engineering students in higher education
target_learning_goals: Understanding how access to GenAI reshapes implicit rules, norms, and educational practices
examples: The article analyzes students using GenAI to 'enhance idea generation' as a shift from purely human-generated ideas to a hybrid approach, indicating changed division of labor and a new implicit rule about ideation tools
key_sources: Tiina Leino Lindell, Christian Stöhr. (2026). The AI disruption in engineering education: an analysis of changing student norms through cultural historical activity theory. Journal of Computing in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12528-025-09488-8

article_title: An Activity-Theoretical Approach to Teacher Professional Development in Pedagogical AI Agent Design
citation: Haiyang Xin, Qiannan Niu, Shuang Li, Yimeng Sun, Ching Sing Chai, Lingyun Huang, Gaowei Chen. (2026). An Activity-Theoretical Approach to Teacher Professional Development in Pedagogical AI Agent Design. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.12934
title: CHAT-SDT diagnostic framework for transformative teacher professional development
description: The framework integrates Engeström's Cultural-Historical Activity Theory with Self-Determination Theory as a replicable diagnostic logic for professional development. The study "adopts Engeström's (2001) activity theory to analyze teachers' AI agent creation as an activity system comprising six interrelated elements: subject, object, tools, rules, community, and division of labor." CHAT diagnoses where structural contradictions exist; SDT explains how those contradictions thwart autonomy, competence, and relatedness, mapping each diagnosed need frustration onto concrete redesign choices. The authors offer it as extending beyond AI contexts.
requirements: Diagnosis of activity system contradictions through systematic analysis of behavioral and interview data before intervention redesign
constraints: In this study researchers acted as interventionists diagnosing contradictions within district-mandated PD constraints, rather than participants collectively identifying contradictions as in pure formative interventions
target_learners: K-12 in-service teachers
target_learning_goals: Sustained creation of pedagogical AI agents aligned with instructional goals
Integration of AI tools with pedagogy and content knowledge (AI-TPACK/IPACK)
examples: Cycle 2 mapped autonomy frustration to choice architecture, competence frustration to progressive scaffolding and embedded AI assistants, and relatedness frustration to community sharing and peer consultation channels.
key_sources: Haiyang Xin, Qiannan Niu, Shuang Li, Yimeng Sun, Ching Sing Chai, Lingyun Huang, Gaowei Chen. (2026). An Activity-Theoretical Approach to Teacher Professional Development in Pedagogical AI Agent Design. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.12934

article_title: A systematic mapping review at the intersection of artificial intelligence and self-regulated learning
citation: Banihashem, S. K., Bond, M., Bergdahl, N., Khosravi, H., & Noroozi, O. (2025). A systematic mapping review at the intersection of artificial intelligence and self-regulated learning. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education, 22(50). https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-025-00548-8
title: Chatti et al.'s Who-What-How-Why framework adapted to map the AI-SRL research intersection
description: The review adopts Chatti et al.'s (2012) learning analytics framework and applies it to AI-supported SRL, structuring the field along four aspects: "Who (stakeholders), What (theory), How (methods), and Why (objectives)". Who covers stakeholder groups targeted; What covers the theoretical frameworks underpinning studies; How covers AI implementation categories such as profiling and prediction, intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive systems and personalization, and assessment and evaluation; Why covers direct impacts on SRL and end outcomes. The review argues the framework captures aspects the prior SMA Grid review omitted, including AI's purposes, methodologies, and underlying theory.
requirements: Studies must be classifiable along the four aspects of stakeholders, theory, implementation, and objectives
constraints: The framework was originally designed for learning analytics and was adapted, with the review distinguishing AI from LA by AI's ability to autonomously adjust to the learner
target_learners: higher education students
K-12 students
educators
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning
examples: The review used the framework to structure four research questions on stakeholders, theoretical frameworks, implementation, and purposes
key_sources: Banihashem, S. K., Bond, M., Bergdahl, N., Khosravi, H., & Noroozi, O. (2025). A systematic mapping review at the intersection of artificial intelligence and self-regulated learning. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education, 22(50). https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-025-00548-8

article_title: Automating Constructive Assessment with Large Language Models: Toward Scalable and Repeated Evaluation of Practical Competence
citation: Satoshi Takahashi, Atsushi Yoshikawa, Megumi Kose, Kenichi Suzuki, Chieko Inoue, Yumi Watanabe, and Mari Sawada. (2026). Automating Constructive Assessment with Large Language Models: Toward Scalable and Repeated Evaluation of Practical Competence. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.25790
title: ChatGPT-based automated HDR assessment system (problem generation, scoring, and feedback pipeline)
description: An LLM-based automated environment built with ChatGPT (GPT-4o) that integrates three prompts—problem generation, scoring, and feedback—into one system handling the full HDR assessment cycle. The scoring and feedback prompts are integrated into one prompt, with "Explanation" and "Good Points" sections outputting the score rationale and feedback. The system generates problems aligned with educational intentions and quickly assesses descriptive tasks focused on knowledge misuse, with reproducibility, immediacy, and low cost.
requirements: A pretest collecting actual descriptive answers from learners to serve as the basis for scoring and feedback prompts
Prompts designed for consistency, educational validity, and explainability
constraints: Some problem and answer data were collected in a previous study (Takahashi et al., 2025)
Validated only with GPT-4o; behavior may differ across LLMs
target_learners: Working adults in business education (MBA-style programs)
target_learning_goals: Detection and explanation of knowledge misuse in practical cases
examples: The generated problem was set at a fictional company, Tsurukame Fitness Inc., with the same paragraph structure and three embedded STP errors as the original problem

article_title: Who Is Solving the Challenge? The Use of ChatGPT in Mathematics and Biology Courses Using Challenge-Based Learning
citation: Elizondo-García ME, Hernández-De la Cerda H, Benavides-García IG, Caratozzolo P and Membrillo-Hernández J (2025) Who is solving the challenge? The use of ChatGPT in mathematics and biology courses using challenge-based learning. Front. Educ. 10:1417642. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2025.1417642
title: ChatGPT-as-starting-point with mandatory cross-validation against academic sources
description: A challenge-based learning activity design in which students use ChatGPT as a starting point for research and then verify its outputs. In the biology course activity on gut microbiota, students gained quick insight from ChatGPT and "were tasked with validating the information derived from ChatGPT by cross-checking it with at least two academic, reliable, verifiable, and current sources." In the mathematics course, ChatGPT acted as a virtual research assistant for scikit-learn topics, with sample prompts provided to guide the research process. The design pairs the tool's immediacy with an explicit validation requirement intended to engage critical evaluation of AI outputs.
requirements: Explicit instruction to validate ChatGPT outputs using formal academic sources
Access to ChatGPT during the activity
constraints: Critical-evaluation survey items (Q11–Q13) received the lowest scores despite the explicit validation instruction, suggesting the design did not strongly foster critical evaluation skills
target_learners: university students in general-education STEM courses across multiple campuses, online delivery
target_learning_goals: disciplinary research skills (e.g., microbiota and nutrition; scikit-learn machine learning algorithms) and critical evaluation of AI-generated information
examples: "Feed your microbiota" activity in Fundamentals of Biological Systems; "Machine Learning Research with ChatGPT" activity in Mathematics and Data Science for Decision Making
key_sources: Elizondo-García ME, Hernández-De la Cerda H, Benavides-García IG, Caratozzolo P and Membrillo-Hernández J (2025) Who is solving the challenge? article_title: Pedagogical Promise and Peril of AI: A Text Mining Analysis of ChatGPT Research Discussions in Programming Education
citation: Grume, J. C., Miranda, J. P. P., De Leon, A. P., Salenga, J. L., Hernandez, H. E., Castro, M. A., Maniago, V. G. M., Canlas, J. D., & Quiambao, J. B. (2026). Pedagogical Promise and Peril of AI: A Text Mining Analysis of ChatGPT Research Discussions in Programming Education. In M. B. Garcia (Ed.), Pedagogical Innovations in Computer Science Education (pp. 305-330). IGI Global Scientific Publishing. https://doi.org/10.4018/979-8-3373-6546-6.ch010
title: Four-theme taxonomy of scholarly discourse on ChatGPT in programming education
description: The chapter organizes the research literature on ChatGPT in programming education into four LDA-derived themes: Pedagogical Use and Classroom Implementation, Student-Centered Learning and Engagement, AI Infrastructure and Human-AI Collaboration, and Assessment, Prompting, and Model Evaluation. The taxonomy maps which scholarly conversations dominate the field, showing research "focus on the classroom and learner experience, while the remaining topics reflect growing attention to institutional and evaluative perspectives." It links representative authors to each theme and serves as a map for researchers and policymakers locating gaps such as assessment design and institutional governance.
requirements: A corpus of open-access publications on ChatGPT and programming education, preprocessed with stopword removal and Porter stemming, analyzed with term frequency, phrase pattern, and LDA topic modeling
constraints: Built from 69 open-access Scopus-indexed documents; topic proportions reflect that corpus and may shift as the literature grows
target_learners: programming education researchers

title: Three-construct framework for measuring challenge navigation in games: challenge approach, challenge response, and general persistence
description: The article organizes in-game motivational behavior into three constructs: "challenge approach, challenge response, and general persistence". Challenge approach covers how players choose challenging situations and code; challenge response covers what players do after failure, such as reflecting on hints or downgrading code; general persistence is "simply the willingness to continue playing the game", without distinguishing easier from harder levels. The framework guided creation of eleven log-based measures validated against a classic persistence task and learning outcomes.
requirements: Requires fine-grained log or screen-recording data from a game that logs level choices, code complexity, attempts, and timing around failures
constraints: The authors note their measures "were confined by the structure and mechanics of this particular game", e.g. gating makes post-failure level choice a challenge-approach rather than challenge-response behavior

motivational behaviors around challenge
examples: Eleven measures in Table 1 were assigned to the three constructs, e.g. Hards Solved Complex (approach), Careful Hint Reads (response), Coding Time Day 2 (general persistence)

article_title: Measuring What Matters Most: Choice-Based Assessments for the Digital Age
citation: Daniel L. Schwartz and Dylan Arena. (2013). Measuring What Matters Most: Choice-Based Assessments for the Digital Age. The MIT Press. http://www.macfound.org
title: Choice as the interpretative framework for learning assessment
description: This framework holds that "Choice, rather than knowledge, should be the interpretative frame within which learning assessments are organized." The authors argue education's fundamental goal is preparing students to act independently and make good choices, so assessments should evaluate learning-relevant choices about whether, what, how, and when to learn. They contend current assessments primarily measure accrued knowledge and skills, which sends the wrong message about what counts as useful learning, and that digital technologies finally make choice-centered assessment possible.
requirements: Assessments must focus on learning-relevant choices such as how and what to learn, not all choices, and must not enforce beliefs outside publicly sponsored education such as political or religious matters
constraints: The authors restrict the framework to learning-relevant choices, explicitly excluding choices outside the purview of education
target_learners: K-12 and higher education students assessed in formal and informal settings
target_learning_goals: Preparing students to make good learning choices and act independently
examples: The Ohno! Has Talent choicelet assesses the choice to engage in critical thinking by tracking which color-mixing charts students choose to believe

article_title: Working memory development from early childhood to adolescence using two nationally representative samples.

title: Childhood is a key window of opportunity—and vulnerability—for working memory development, suggesting early timing of WM-supporting efforts
description: Because WM grows most rapidly during childhood, the authors argue this period "may provide a window of opportunity during which the effects of interventions might be the most effective", while also being a time when WM development "might be particularly vulnerable to the effects of negative environmental settings". This supports prioritizing WM-supporting practices and environments in early childhood and elementary education.
requirements: Identification of contextual predictors of WM growth to target supports effectively
constraints: The intervention-timing implication is the authors' interpretation; the study measured normative growth, not intervention effects

target_learning_goals: supporting working memory growth underlying learning and academic skill development
examples: The study's fitted trajectories showed the steepest digit span growth across ages 3–10, leveling off in late childhood before a brief early-adolescent uptick.

title: Cattell–Horn–Carroll (CHC) hierarchical model of intelligence as an organizing framework for creative cognition
description: The article uses modern CHC theory, described as "an emerging consensus on the structure of cognitive abilities based on decades of factor-analytic research", which "conceptualizes intelligence as a hierarchical structure of abilities, from narrow (specific abilities, such as inductive reasoning) to broad (global abilities, such as fluid intelligence) to general (g)". Three broad factors—Gf, Gc, and Gr—were modeled as latent variables to predict two kinds of metaphor production, extending the CHC framework into the study of creative cognition.

raters blind to each other's scores and participants' other data

adult learners

citation: Berhenke, Amanda; Miller, Alison L.; Brown, Eleanor; Seifer, Ronald; Dickstein, Susan. (2011). Observed Emotional and Behavioral Indicators of Motivation Predict School Readiness in Head Start Graduates. Early childhood research quarterly. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecresq.2011.04.001
title: Observational challenge-task assessment of motivation with AFFEX-adapted emotion coding and project-developed task behavior codes
description: This assessment consists of five puzzle tasks and a trivia game adapted from Smiley and Dweck (1994), including impossible puzzles and failure-feedback trivia, videotaped and coded for emotion and task behavior. "Emotion (adapted from the AFFEX coding system; Izard, Dougherty, & Hembree, 1989) and task behavior states (a coding system developed for this project) were coded independently by student coding teams using The Observer XT software system." Children were continuously coded into seven mutually exclusive emotion states and three task behavior states, plus discrete events (pride, shame, frustration, hostility, help-seeking, competence). Reliability was established via intraclass correlations on 10% of tapes.

constraints: Rare events such as shame and hostility were coded by group consensus and did not occur with sufficient frequency for reliability analyses

Head Start graduates in low-income families
target_learning_goals: assessment of motivation via observed emotion expression and task engagement during academic challenge

article_title: Physical activity and creativity of children and youths

description: The article advances the account that childhood is a valuable period for developing creative skills because cognitive abilities attributed to prefrontal cortex function are required for creativity, and the prefrontal cortex does not completely mature until the early 20s. It concludes that "optimal physical activity is required during childhood for developing thinking process", positioning physical activity — especially active play — as supportive of cognitive development alongside previously reported links to intelligence and emotional quotients.

constraints: The account rests on cross-sectional correlations; the article states many factors related to creativity remain and more information is needed to clarify other factors

cognitive function development
examples: The article cites cross-sectional studies in which increased physical activity was associated with higher intelligence quotient in 135 Saudi high school students and higher emotional quotient in 599 Taiwanese college students

citation: Yifat Ben-David Kolikant, Omri Hadar, Asaf Salman. (2025). Talk to the machine: Unleashing the potential of AI to scale dialogic education and reduce polarization. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09461-8
title: Embed chatbot-preceded dialogic practice within macro-scripts as a preparatory phase for peer discussion on contentious topics
description: The article argues the conversation with the machine "should not replace the talk with humans" and should be "embedded in broader macro-scripts" supporting peer discussions on identity-related contentious topics. As a preparatory phase, the chatbot can equip participants with relevant content knowledge, help them identify weaknesses in their arguments, introduce alternative perspectives attuned to their utterances, and let students practice switching roles, arguing for a claim and then against it.

constraints: The chatbot is positioned as a preparatory phase rather than a replacement for human discussion; bias and negative tone issues persist (Fig. 4).

article_title: Developing a ‘big picture’: Effects of collaborative construction of multimodal representations in history
citation: Maaike E. Prangsma, Carla A. M. Van Boxtel, Gellof Kanselaar. (2008). Developing a 'big picture': Effects of collaborative construction of multimodal representations in history. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-007-9026-5
title: Chronological-conceptual frame of reference as the knowledge base for historical reasoning
description: The article frames history learning around a chronological frame of reference, defined as "the knowledge base that is used when reasoning about the past". It consists of three components: knowledge of historical phenomena (events, structures, themes), knowledge of temporal and causal relations between phenomena, and knowledge of concepts describing phenomena and relations. The study's multimodal tasks were designed to combine all three components, and the timeline condition additionally visualised temporal relations across tasks. The framework draws on Leinhardt's typology of historical phenomena (events, structures, themes, metasystems).

constraints: A timeline with dates and textual descriptions only visualises temporal relationships and does not show underlying causal relationships

understanding of historical phenomena, temporal and causal relations, and historical concepts

article_title: Investigating construct validity of cognitive load measurement using single-item subjective rating scales
citation: Schuessler, K., Fischer, V., & Walpuski, M. (2025). Investigating construct validity of cognitive load measurement using single-item subjective rating scales. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09692-6
title: Researchers must deliberately choose between invested mental effort and perceived task difficulty items and state at which point and how frequently cognitive load is measured
description: Because the two dominant single-item cognitive load ratings capture different aspects of overall load, the article advises that "researchers should therefore discuss carefully which item they use and how this may limit the results of their study". It further advises "to precisely examine at which point and how frequently cognitive load is measured as delayed ratings are closely related to more demanding items within a set of items". The principle applies whenever single-item subjective ratings are used as an indicator of overall cognitive load.
requirements: Researchers must decide and justify which single-item rating (invested mental effort or perceived task difficulty) is used, since the two do not measure the same construct.
The timing and frequency of measurement must be specified, because delayed ratings are closely related to the more demanding items in a set.
constraints: Single-item subjective ratings provide only an impression of overall cognitive load and do not differentiate intrinsic from extraneous load.
Delayed single ratings are affected by the most demanding item, so changes in load during a task set are better captured by repeated measurement.
target_learners: secondary school students
learners in large-scale classroom or test settings
target_learning_goals: valid measurement of perceived cognitive load during task performance
examples: In the reanalyzed study, cognitive load was rated after each of 32 tasks (sets of four items) using adapted 7-point versions of the Paas (1992) mental effort item and the Marcus et al. (1996) perceived task difficulty item.

citation: O'Hare, S., Kajamaa, A., Conn, R., & Gormley, G. (2025). SimLab: an intervention to promote expansive learning and organisational change in team-based emergency care simulation. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09734-7
title: Cultural-historical activity theory and expansive learning as a design and analysis framework for interprofessional in-situ simulation
description: The article operationalises cultural-historical activity theory (CHAT) as both the design lens and analytical framework for simulation. CHAT analyses collective human activity through an activity system of six elements — subject, object, tools, rules, community, division of labour — and "enables a collaborative enquiry into systemic contradictions". Expansive learning describes how participants collectively construct a new expanded object for their activity, moving through seven learning actions from questioning to consolidation. The authors chose CHAT because it views practice and learning as inseparable and suits workplace-based interprofessional training.
requirements: Requires analysis of group discussions using the activity system model as the unit of analysis and the seven expansive learning actions
constraints: Second-generation CHAT was employed; the framework was applied in one general practice setting

target_learning_goals: collective preparedness for paediatric emergencies
organisational change in emergency care practice
examples: The SimLab sessions were each designed to incorporate one to two expansive learning actions, with the activity system model introduced as a second stimulus

title: CHC theory definition of spatial ability as visual processing (Gv) with eleven first-order spatial factors in three categories
description: Within the CHC theory, spatial ability is the second-order Gv (visual processing) factor, defined as the ability to make use of simulated mental imagery to solve problems, with the empirical definition being the first-order factors that load on it. The article reports that "In total, 11 first-order factors are shown to load on spatial ability in the CHC theory", grouped into spatial skills (e.g. visualisation, speeded rotation), perceptual factors (e.g. perceptual alternations), and memory factors (e.g. visual memory). Table 1 prints definitions for each factor.

article_title: Beyond the “Wow” Factor: Using Generative AI for Increasing Generative Sense-Making
citation: Guido Makransky, Ban M. Shiwalia, Tue Herlau, Steven Blurton. (2025). Beyond the "Wow" Factor: Using Generative AI for Increasing Generative Sense-Making. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10039-x
title: ChatTutor: a theory-informed GenAI chatbot that scaffolds the generative learning activity of teaching
description: ChatTutor is a student-focused GenAI chatbot built on generative learning theory, in which "The ChatTutor chatbot engages students in personalized written conversations based on the course slides and texts and responds to address the specific answers provided by students and correcting any misconceptions or gaps in knowledge." Its interface presents self-explanation prompts developed in a workshop with instructors one at a time, lets students respond and ask follow-up questions, and displays specific feedback helping students evaluate and improve their responses, while a side panel shows targeted course knowledge the chatbot references. It simulates a student-tutor interaction, intervening when misconceptions are evident or help is requested, and allows escalating questions to a human instructor.
requirements: A targeted knowledge bank linked to the course slides and texts so the chatbot's prompts and feedback reference the taught content
constraints: In the studies the generative activity lasted approximately 15 minutes in Study 1 and at least 25 minutes in Study 2, and the tool was evaluated within authentic course lessons rather than as standalone study support

high school psychology students

self-explaining and teaching as generative learning activities
examples: In Study 1, two exercise classes used ChatTutor, two used an identical interface linked to ChatGPT-4, and three received teaching-as-usual; in Study 2 the design was replicated with 234 high school students and a re-studying control

article_title: A systematic review of the role of learning analytics in enhancing feedback practices in higher education
citation: Seyyed Kazem Banihashem, Omid Noroozi, Stan van Ginkel, Leah P. Macfadyen, Harm J.A. Biemans. (2022). A systematic review of the role of learning analytics in enhancing feedback practices in higher education. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2022.100489
title: Four-dimension LA reference model (what, how, why, who) guiding the review of LA for feedback
description: The review adopts Chatti et al.'s (2012) reference model in which "LA consists of four dimensions including (1) what (what types of data does the system capture and analyze), (2) how (how does the system perform analytics), (3) why (for what reasons does the system gather and analyze data), and (4) who (who is served by the analytics)". This framework structures the review's coding scheme and four research questions, and underpins the conceptual framework the authors propose to guide implementation of LA for feedback systems in higher education.
requirements: Included studies must report findings, implications or evidence addressing at least one of the four dimensions (data, methods, objectives, stakeholders) for LA feedback in higher education
constraints: The review restricts scope to peer-reviewed empirical studies in higher education settings published 2011–2022, excluding conceptual studies and K-12 contexts
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: improving feedback practices and feedback-supported learning in technology-mediated higher education environments
examples: The review coded all 46 papers in ATLAS.ti against the four categories (what, how, why, who), achieving 91 percent inter-rater agreement (κ = 0.84).

This principle guides study design in educational research on student characteristics and achievement.

article_title: The Impasse on Gender Differences in Intelligence: a Meta-Analysis on WISC Batteries
citation: D. Giofrè · K. Allen · E. Toffalini · S. Caviola. (2022). The Impasse on Gender Differences in Intelligence: a Meta-Analysis on WISC Batteries. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09705-1
title: CHC theory and the cross-battery approach as the framework for locating WISC gender differences across ability levels
description: The article adopts the Cattell-Horn-Carroll (CHC) theory and the cross-battery approach as its organizing framework, in which "the CHC model divides cognitive abilities into different levels": the g-factor at the top, broad abilities (gF, gV, gC, gSM, gS, gQ) in the middle, and narrow abilities at the base. WISC subtests are assigned to broad factors by their CHC loadings, allowing female/male differences to be estimated at factor and subtest levels rather than only on FSIQ. The framework also motivates comparing results across WISC battery versions.
requirements: WISC subtests must be classifiable into CHC broad factors by their loadings, as the article codes them (e.g. Block design to gV, Coding to gS).
constraints: The article did not calculate a gQ factor because only one subtest (arithmetic) measured it, making the factor unnecessary in its words.
target_learners: school-aged children assessed with the WISC
target_learning_goals: accurate assessment of cognitive ability differences between genders in children
examples: The meta-analysis used subtests such as vocabulary and information as indicators of gC, and matrix reasoning and picture concepts as indicators of gF, fitting separate models per factor.

article_title: Motivation and Personality: Current Integrative Perspectives and the Way Ahead
citation: Lisa Bardach, Luise von Keyserlingk, Jacque S. Eccles. (2026). Motivation and Personality: Current Integrative Perspectives and the Way Ahead. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10147-2
title: Characteristic adaptations as the bridge between personality traits and educational motivation
description: Drawing on McAdams and colleagues, the article treats characteristic adaptations (e.g., motives, goals, plans, strivings, strategies, values, self-images) as intermediate constructs between personality traits and specific behaviors within a situation, and describes them as capturing "how traits interact with changing situational demands". Because these adaptations "closely map onto the social ecology of everyday life", they include everyday learning situations. The article argues educational psychology's clearly defined motivational constructs can specify the broad category of characteristic adaptations, which personality researchers have criticized as vague, and illustrates how a conscientious student may adopt mastery goals when facing demanding learning materials.
requirements: Personality traits are understood as relatively enduring and automatic patterns of thoughts, feelings, and behaviors, not as completely fixed and unaffected by experience
constraints: The article notes the characteristic adaptation perspective is somewhat limited in that personality usually remains restricted to the trait level
target_learners: school and university students
target_learning_goals: goal adoption, learning engagement, and learning behaviors in demanding situations
examples: A highly conscientious student facing difficult learning materials activates goals conducive to engaging with them, such as mastery goals of really understanding the materials

article_title: The Value of Pretend Play for Social Competence in Early Childhood: A Meta-analysis
citation: Smits-van der Nat, M., van der Wilt, F., Meeter, M., & van der Veen, C. (2024). The Value of Pretend Play for Social Competence in Early Childhood: A Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09884-z
title: Vygotsky's cultural-historical activity theory account of pretend play as a context for social competence development
description: Cultural-historical activity theory (CHAT) holds that children develop higher mental functions, such as social competence, through collaborative participation in socio-cultural practices. In early childhood settings these practices (a restaurant, supermarket, bookshop, or museum) are often imitated within pretend play, where children imitate adults engaging in socially desirable behavior and practice negotiating play themes, social roles, and rules. The meta-analysis frames its hypothesis in these terms and interprets the age moderation as possible confirmation of the CHAT tenet that the 3–6 year period is crucial.
requirements: Engagement in pretend play in which children re-enact the surrounding socio-cultural world, typically within early childhood education and care contexts
constraints: The article states empirical support for the causal conjecture is limited and that no claims of causality can be drawn from the correlational evidence
target_learners: Children aged 3–8 years in early childhood education and care
target_learning_goals: Social competence, including negotiating play themes, social roles, and rules and solving peer conflicts
examples: The meta-analysis of 34 studies tested the CHAT-derived hypothesis that pretend play is positively related to children's social competence

article_title: Experiencing fear appeals as a challenge or a threat influences attainment value and academic self-efficacy
citation: The appraisal of fear appeals as a challenge or a threat influences a subsequent decline or increase in attainment value and academic self-efficacy. (2014). https://eric.ed.gov/?q=appraisal+of+fear+appeals+challenge+threat+attainment+value+academic+self-efficacy
title: Challenge and threat appraisal framework for classroom fear appeals grounded in EVT and control-value theory
description: The article frames teacher fear appeals prior to high-stakes examinations as appraised on two dimensions: primary appraisal of personal relevance and secondary appraisal of response options. It states that "A challenge appraisal occurs when the fear appeal is judged as being relevant and the student believes that they can respond effectively to the demands posed in the message", accompanied by positive emotions such as hope, whereas a threat appraisal occurs when demands are believed to outweigh one's ability to respond, accompanied by anxiety. Attainment value (from expectancy-value theory) establishes relevance and academic self-efficacy establishes response options, and a CVT feedback loop from emotions back to control and value beliefs explains how appraisals subsequently change those beliefs.
requirements: Fear appeals must be personally relevant to students for appraisal processes to operate
Constructs should be operationalised at the same level of domain specificity (here subject-specific, per the matching-specificity principle)
constraints: The study examined student-level appraisals only and did not measure actual teacher behaviour such as frequency or strength of fear appeals
Only attainment value was examined; other subjective task values, in particular cost, were not included
target_learners: Secondary school students in the final two years of education preparing for high-stakes examinations
target_learning_goals: Maintaining attainment value and academic self-efficacy in the run-up to high-stakes examinations
examples: Students with high attainment value and high academic self-efficacy (+1 SD) at T1 were projected to report a challenge score of 4.17 and a threat score of 2.56, with above-average T3 academic self-efficacy (3.86) and attainment value (4.24).

article_title: Pedagogical psychology of report.
citation: Lipmann, O. (1911). Pedagogical Psychology of Report. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://archive.org
title: Childhood imagination as reality: imagined content initially bears the character of a memory-image
description: The article proposes a fundamental characteristic of the childish imagination as a further cause of faulty reports: "everything that is imagined is imagined as real." Whether an image comes as a memory-image, from fancy, or from suggestion, it at first plays the role of a real experience for the child, so imagined fillings of memory gaps are reported as actual memories. The author limits this crude formulation to the very small child, since accumulating experience teaches that fancy differs from reality, but even school children's recognition remains relatively little developed.
requirements: Explains wrong reports that arise when children fill gaps in memory with material from fancy, custom, or suggestion
constraints: The author states the crude formulation holds only for the very small child, and that the role of fancy does not admit of experimental treatment
target_learners: children
target_learning_goals: accurate reporting of past experiences
examples: The author cites observation-based material on fancy as a source of wrong reports, noting it cannot be treated experimentally.

citation: Şimşek, E., Xenidou-Dervou, I., Hunter, J., Gillon Dowens, M., Pang, J., Lee, Y., McNeil, N., Kirkland, P., & Jones, I. (2021). Factors Associated with Children's Understanding of Mathematical Equivalence: An Investigation across Six Countries. https://figshare.com/s/78625a6b0061200db6b7

description: The change-resistance account of McNeil and Alibali (2005), described in this article's literature review, proposes that "excessive practice with only a traditional arithmetic presentation" reinforces three operational patterns (answer blank after equals sign, use all given numbers, equals sign means 'do something') and hinders performance on complex equations. The present study tested a textbook-format implication of this account and found no relation with equivalence understanding.

constraints: The article's own large-scale data found no relation between non-traditional textbook practice and equivalence understanding, qualifying the account's textbook prediction

article_title: Tests for originality.

description: A battery of twelve individual and group-administered tests for originality, five devised in the Northwestern University psychological laboratory and seven adapted or modified from prior tests, covering word-building, picture writing, analogues, puzzles, completion, economic prophecy, code translation, invention, and novel hypothetical situations. Instructions were given orally and by placard, and a constructed time-keeping device let subjects record their own time. The article states, "the following twelve were selected and modified for subsequent use." Scores ranged from timed solutions to graded originality of suggestions, and each student's final group rank was the median of his twelve ranks.

The article states this "allows for the development of easily implementable strategies to improve academic performance without needing specialized resting places equipped with beds". This keeps the ecological character of the intervention, with lessons delivered by the regular teacher.

citation: Hongxin Yan, Fuhua Lin & Kinshuk. (2021). Including Learning Analytics in the Loop of Self-Paced Online Course Learning Design. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education (2021) 31:878–895. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00225-z
title: Embedding check-point activities in a course so learning data are generated regardless of how and where students learn
description: This course-level design pattern addresses SPOL's data-generation problem: students who learn offline or log in irregularly leave little learning data. title: A dual-focus framework for preparing ChatGPT prompts for training, distinguishing general LLM prompting principles from application-specific pedagogical principles

article_title: A Comparison of Model-Tracing and Constraint-Based Intelligent Tutoring Paradigms
citation: Viswanathan Kodaganallur, Rob R. Weitz, David Rosenthal. (2005). A Comparison of Model-Tracing and Constraint-Based Intelligent Tutoring Paradigms. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197305
title: Choose between model-tracing and constraint-based tutoring paradigms by assessing solution information richness and goal-structure complexity
description: When selecting an intelligent tutoring paradigm, assess the problem domain first: use constraint-based modelling when the solution itself is information-rich and development effort must be minimized; prefer model tracing when targeted, high-quality remediation matters, especially with complex solution process goal structures. The article derives this guidance from building both tutor types for one domain.
requirements: A judgment of whether the solution itself is rich in information, and of the complexity of the solution process goal structure
constraints: The constraint-based paradigm is feasible only for domains in which the solution itself is rich in information
target_learners: students in domains suitable for intelligent tutoring, such as statistical hypothesis testing
target_learning_goals: effective tutoring support including targeted remediation
examples: The authors built both tutor types for statistical hypothesis testing and concluded the two domain characteristics are key to choosing the appropriate approach.
key_sources: Viswanathan Kodaganallur, Rob R. Weitz, David Rosenthal. (2005). A Comparison of Model-Tracing and Constraint-Based Intelligent Tutoring Paradigms. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197305

article_title: Benefits of Virtual Characters in Computer Based Learning Environments: Claims and Evidence
citation: Agneta Gulz. (2004). Benefits of Virtual Characters in Computer Based Learning Environments: Claims and Evidence. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 14, pp. 313-334. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197309
title: Character-enhanced learning environments as a research focus
description: The article focuses on character-enhanced systems, defined as electronic learning environments to which virtual characters have been added. The approach is motivated by the high priority that pedagogical theory gives to social components of learning. The article provides a systematic overview of proposed benefits and examines the empirical evidence for them.
requirements: Electronic learning environments that have been enhanced with virtual characters.
target_learners: learners in computer-based learning environments
target_learning_goals: social components of learning
key_sources: Agneta Gulz. (2004). Benefits of Virtual Characters in Computer Based Learning Environments: Claims and Evidence. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 14, pp. 313-334. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197309

article_title: Choice Architecture for Nudges to Support Constructive Learning in Active Video Watching
citation: Vania Dimitrova & Antonija Mitrovic. (2021). Choice Architecture for Nudges to Support Constructive Learning in Active Video Watching. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00263-1
title: Choice architecture framework for personalised nudges to promote active video watching
description: The paper proposes what it calls the first choice architecture framework for personalised nudges in learning environments, defining target behaviours (e.g. making comments, noticing important segments, reflecting, linking to personal experience), observed behaviours to correct (e.g. watching without commenting, shallow comments), and nudges as interaction games. It adopts the Münscher et al. nudge taxonomy of decision information, decision structure and decision assistance, and adopts Michie et al.'s behaviour-change principles of capability, motivation and opportunity. The authors state: "Our work is the first attempt to devise choice architecture for personalised nudges to improve learning", using a data-driven, learner-sourcing approach where past learners' behaviour shapes future learning experiences.
requirements: A learner model to detect observed behaviours where nudges may be needed, since the framework states that detecting unhelpful situations "requires a learner model"
constraints: The framework is outlined within the context of video-based informal learning and was operationalised in AVW-Space for pitch presentation skills
target_learners: university students (undergraduate, Master and PhD) learning transferable skills from videos
target_learning_goals: transferable skills such as delivering pitch presentations, including noticing key skill elements and reflecting on personal experience
examples: Example interaction games include DI_visible (heatmap of high-attention intervals), DS_increase-effort (prompting unused aspects), and DA_reminder (prompting a summary after watching without commenting)
key_sources: Vania Dimitrova & Antonija Mitrovic. (2021). Choice Architecture for Nudges to Support Constructive Learning in Active Video Watching. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00263-1

article_title: The impact of high-immersion virtual reality on anatomy learning, enjoyment, presence, and cognitive load
citation: Kaplan-Rakowski, R., Norton, S., & Wojdynski, T. (2026). The impact of high-immersion virtual reality on anatomy learning, enjoyment, presence, and cognitive load. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10676-1
title: Channel VR immersion toward productive cognitive activity aligned with learning goals
description: The article argues that immersion alone does not produce learning; instructional design must direct it. It states that "instructional methods should channel immersion toward productive cognitive activity (e.g., guided manipulation, prompts for self-explanation)" and that improved VR designs "may therefore need to structure interaction more explicitly around core learning goals rather than around free exploration alone." This principle follows from the finding that VR learners enjoyed the lesson more yet learned less than video learners.
requirements: Explicit alignment between interactive VR features and subject-specific learning goals; structured interaction rather than free exploration
constraints: The article frames this as needed for factual, recall-oriented tasks such as anatomy labeling; VR may show advantages for other task types
target_learners: college students
novice learners of anatomy
target_learning_goals: factual and spatial STEM knowledge
examples: The study's VR condition allowed free exploration of a holographic heart, and the authors suggest that designs structured around guided manipulation and self-explanation prompts may better support learning
key_sources: Kaplan-Rakowski, R., Norton, S., & Wojdynski, T. (2026). The impact of high-immersion virtual reality on anatomy learning, enjoyment, presence, and cognitive load. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10676-1

article_title: A classification tool to foster self-regulated learning with generative artificial intelligence by applying self-determination theory: a case of ChatGPT
citation: Chiu, T. K. F. (2024). A classification tool to foster self-regulated learning with generative artificial intelligence by applying self-determination theory: a case of ChatGPT. Education Tech Research Dev, 72, 2401–2416. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10366-w
title: Classification tool of 20 ChatGPT learning activities with descriptions and consensus mappings to SDT needs and SRL phases
description: The article's main artifact is a classification tool listing 20 ChatGPT-based learning activities, each with a description and a consensus rating of which SDT need and SRL phase it serves (Tables 1 and 2). Activities include when students "search information, get examples, check their answers, generate review questions to check for their understanding, create new problems for practice, create challenging problems, get insight into complex problems, ask ideas for their improvement, make lists or outlines," and more. It is intended to help researchers replicate intervention studies and help teachers adapt activities.
requirements: Activities carry consensus-established labels, descriptions, and explanations of their impact on needs and phases, refined across three Delphi rounds.
constraints: The authors note many activities are not typical or less common teaching practices, so teachers would need to modify them for their own teaching.
target_learners: School students in Hong Kong across primary and secondary academic levels
target_learning_goals: Self-regulated learning across forethought, performance, and self-reflection phases
SDT needs satisfaction (autonomy, competence, relatedness)
examples: Teachers and researchers can use the tool to conduct intervention research on whether ChatGPT fosters the SRL process, and developers may use the activities to improve educational ChatGPT development.
key_sources: Chiu, T. K. F. (2024). A classification tool to foster self-regulated learning with generative artificial intelligence by applying self-determination theory: a case of ChatGPT. Education Tech Research Dev, 72, 2401–2416. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10366-w

article_title: A classification tool to foster self-regulated learning with generative artificial intelligence by applying self-determination theory: a case of ChatGPT
citation: Chiu, T. K. F. (2024). A classification tool to foster self-regulated learning with generative artificial intelligence by applying self-determination theory: a case of ChatGPT. Education Tech Research Dev, 72, 2401–2416. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10366-w
title: Pair ChatGPT-based activities with teacher needs support, since ChatGPT alone cannot satisfy every student need at every SRL phase
description: Because the consensus mappings show ChatGPT activities leave relatedness and autonomy unsatisfied in some SRL phases, the article recommends combining digital and teacher support: "To fully utilize each student’s SRL potential, ChatGPT and the teacher should collaborate." Teachers provide direction and guidance for school children who are still developing, complementing the instant, tailored feedback ChatGPT offers.
requirements: Teachers with well-researched needs-support practices who can provide direction and guidance alongside ChatGPT activities.
constraints: The article states the classification may not simply apply to classroom instruction because the aims and contexts differ, since the study looked only at digital support rather than blended learning.
target_learners: School students, including young students still developing self-regulation
target_learning_goals: Full use of each student's SRL potential
SDT needs satisfaction across all three phases
examples: The discussion recommends collaboration for young students' SRL, noting teachers must provide direction and guidance because school children are still developing.
