article_title: Empowering children online: a holistic skills framework for cybersecurity
citation: Nicolai B. Plintz, Dirk Ifenthaler. (2026). Empowering children online: a holistic skills framework for cybersecurity. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10565-z
title: Formulate children's cybersecurity competencies as actionable 'Children can…' capability statements rather than theoretical knowledge
description: When extracting skills for the framework, the authors standardized heterogeneous source formulations into actionable capability statements. The article reports: "Items that originally described knowledge or awareness were reformulated as demonstrable capabilities (e.g., “Children can recognize that malware exists”), while action-oriented statements were maintained as “Children can [perform action]”." This ensures the framework focuses on practical abilities rather than theoretical knowledge, supporting direct translation into age-appropriate learning objectives for curriculum designers and teachers.
requirements: Source statements must be reformulated while preserving the original intent and meaning of each study's findings
constraints: The reformulation was applied to skills for children aged 8–13 in the cybersecurity domain
target_learners: Children aged 8–13
target_learning_goals: Practical cybersecurity abilities such as recognizing threats, protecting data, and responding to incidents
examples: Knowledge statements like 'should know that malware exists' became 'Children can recognize that malware exists' during the revision process
key_sources: Nicolai B. Plintz, Dirk Ifenthaler. (2026). Empowering children online: a holistic skills framework for cybersecurity. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10565-z

article_title: Computational thinking beyond coding: exploring student computational practices while playing and modifying a socio-scientific simulation game with integrated computational tools
citation: Marianthi Grizioti. (2025). Computational thinking beyond coding: exploring student computational practices while playing and modifying a socio-scientific simulation game with integrated computational tools. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10477-y
title: ChoiCo environment and CT-Chef socio-scientific simulation game
description: ChoiCo (Choices with Consequences) is a web-based open access game authoring environment with a Play Mode for choice-driven simulation games and a Design Mode offering three interconnected computational tools: an editable database of game fields and choices, a map editor connected to the database, and three block-based coding workspaces for game mechanics. CT-Chef is a game created for this study dealing with managing a sustainable, health-promoting restaurant, where choices affect five game fields including money, healthy food and customers per day.
requirements: Design Mode access to the database, map editor and coding workspaces for modification and creation activities
constraints: Student games had to maintain the initial game mechanics of surviving as long as possible via map-based choices
target_learners: middle school students aged 12-14
target_learning_goals: CT practices through game play, modification and design
data editing and systems reasoning
examples: The game extends an older game called Eating Out used in a prior pilot study, and was played in a school computer laboratory by 7 groups
key_sources: Marianthi Grizioti. (2025). Computational thinking beyond coding: exploring student computational practices while playing and modifying a socio-scientific simulation game with integrated computational tools. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10477-y

article_title: A proposed methodology for investigating student-chatbot interaction patterns in giving peer feedback
citation: Michael Pin-Chuan Lin, Daniel H. Chang, Philip H. Winne. (2025). A proposed methodology for investigating student-chatbot interaction patterns in giving peer feedback. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10408-3
title: Chatbot DD: a Rasa-based, CAM-grounded chatbot for coaching peer feedback on essay outlines
description: DD is a task-oriented chatbot built on the open-source Rasa framework (rasa_core 0.11.12, rasa_core_sdk 0.11.5, rasa_nlu 0.13.7) with a web chatroom interface in which students mainly interacted by clicking buttons. The authors state: "We developed the chatbot based on the four components of CAM: content, methods, sequence, and sociology (Collins et al., 1991)." DD teaches four feedback types (constructive suggestions, positive comments, negative comments, questions for improvement), checks understanding with comprehension-checking questions, praises correct answers, then guides revision of fabricated feedback on a sample outline.
requirements: A fallback action for unprocessable input, participatory refinement with the course instructor and teaching staff, and training data for the NLU (about 200 thesis statements)
constraints: The article states the small training set limited NLU accuracy and the chatbot still sometimes failed to identify intents; students mainly used buttons rather than natural language
target_learners: first-year undergraduate educational psychology students
target_learning_goals: understanding and giving the four types of effective peer feedback
examples: In a 50-minute tutorial, each participant was randomly assigned one of five fabricated outlines and its substandard feedback sheet, learned about feedback types with DD, then revised the sheet with DD's guidance
key_sources: Michael Pin-Chuan Lin, Daniel H. Chang, Philip H. Winne. (2025). A proposed methodology for investigating student-chatbot interaction patterns in giving peer feedback. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10408-3

article_title: Assessing aspects of children's written grammar: automating the process
citation: C.E. Holdich, R.G. Holdich and P.W.H. Chung. (2002). Assessing aspects of children's written grammar: automating the process. Computers and Education, Vol 39, pp37-50. http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/2.5/
title: Check Text program: a Visual Basic Script text-analysis tool measuring ten grammar indicators in children's writing
description: The Check Text program, written in Visual Basic Script, supplies statistical information about children's story texts across ten indicators covering vocabulary, syntax and punctuation, including total story length, type-token ratio of the first 100 words, common verbs, words over five letters, adverbs, 'and' and other basic connectives, simple sentence starters, mean sentence length, and commas relative to sentence length. It was created because existing text analysis programs 'are targeted at the way adults write rather than children'. The program's output was compared to examiners' written interpretations of each story.
requirements: Features analysed must be made specifically relevant to children's writing and presented in a way that is meaningful to teachers and children
constraints: A complete linguistic analysis was not undertaken; information about subordinate clause types and adjectival expansion is absent
The formative study used only 12 publicly available examiner-commented stories
target_learners: Year 6 children (aged 11) at Key Stage 2
target_learning_goals: written grammar: sentence construction, vocabulary and punctuation development
examples: Applied to 12 SATs stories spanning National Curriculum levels 2c to 5+, the computer successfully distinguished positive and negative grammar features within these texts
key_sources: C.E. Holdich, R.G. Holdich and P.W.H. Chung. (2002). Assessing aspects of children's written grammar: automating the process. Computers and Education, Vol 39, pp37-50. http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/2.5/

citation: Jara, I., Claro, M., Hinostroza, J. E., San Martin Gutiérrez, E., Rodríguez, P., Cabello, T., Ibieta, A., & Labbé, C. (2015). Understanding factors related to Chilean students' digital skills: A mixed methods analysis. Computers & Education, 88, 387-398. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2015.07.016
title: National standardized digital skills test for Chilean 10th-grade students
description: The study measured students' digital skills with a national standardized test administered to 10th-grade Chilean students. The abstract states the study aimed "to identify and characterize factors related to the digital skills of 10th grade Chilean students, as measured by a national standardized test." The test provided the quantitative outcome for the hierarchical linear model and the basis for selecting high- and low-performing students for the case study.
requirements: Administered as a national standardized test to 10th-grade students to yield comparable digital skills scores.
target_learners: 10th-grade Chilean secondary students
target_learning_goals: Digital literacy and digital skills
examples: Used as the outcome measure in the hierarchical linear model analysis of factors explaining student performance.

article_title: Improving children's written grammar and style: revising and editing with HARRY
citation: C.E. Holdich, P.W.H. Chung and R.G. Holdich. (2004). Improving children's written grammar and style: revising and editing with HARRY. Computers & Education, Vol 42, pp1-23. https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/2.5/
title: CHECK TEXT: a utility tool quantifying twelve aspects of children's written grammar and style
description: CHECK TEXT is a utility tool that "calculates and interprets quantitative data" on children's stories. A previous study demonstrated that it "distinguishes strengths and weaknesses in 12 aspects of children's written grammar and style", covering story length, punctuation (full stops and commas), sentence construction (basic connectives, simple sentence starters, sentence length) and vocabulary (variety and sophistication). Scores are mapped onto three assessment categories - poor, fair and good - using boundaries set from an earlier sample of stories.
requirements: Assessment boundaries calibrated against the original sample stories from Holdich, Holdich and Chung (2002), since the significance of scores is not obvious without that reference
constraints: Story length is capped in practice by lesson time in the evaluation; the article reports thresholds (e.g. basic connectives above 0.8% of total words) as empirically determined for HARRY's detection rather than for CHECK TEXT
target_learners: Primary school children (8-11 years) writing narratives
target_learning_goals: Quantitative assessment of written grammar and style features
examples: CHECK TEXT scored each control story and each of the three stages of the HARRY-assisted stories in the four case studies

article_title: Meta-Analysis on the Effects of Teaching Methods on Academic Performance in Chemistry
citation: Sugano, S. G. C., & Nabua, E. B. (2020). Meta-Analysis on the Effects of Teaching Methods on Academic Performance in Chemistry. International Journal of Instruction, 13(2), 881-894. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2020.13259a
title: Nine-category taxonomy of chemistry teaching methods contrasted with traditional instruction
description: The article organizes chemistry education interventions into nine treatment categories used as the independent variable of the meta-analysis: inquiry-based learning; manipulative, models and multiple representations; cooperative learning; technology-aided instruction; individualized instruction; problem-based learning; project-based learning; combination learning; and multicultural education. Identified teaching methods were "cast into treatment categories that act as the independent variable of this study", with academic performance as the dependent variable. The taxonomy frames innovative methods collectively against "the traditional teaching method".
requirements: Qualified primary studies must report effect sizes or statistical details sufficient to compute them (means, standard deviations, sample sizes, t, f, p values, ANOVA tables, degrees of freedom)
constraints: Studies limited to secondary chemistry, conducted in the Philippines, completed 2005–2016, with experimental or quasi-experimental designs
target_learners: secondary chemistry students in the Philippines
target_learning_goals: academic performance in secondary chemistry
examples: The 51 qualified studies were coded and plotted into mapping matrices by treatment category, and category mean effect sizes were ranked to identify the most influential methods

article_title: The Effect of Student-Centred Methods and Techniques on Primary School Students' Mathematics Achievement: A Meta-Analysis Study
citation: Hakan Ulum, Songül Tümkaya. (2022). The effect of student-centred methods and techniques on primary school students' mathematics achievement: A meta-analysis study. Malikussaleh Journal of Mathematics Learning (MJML). https://ojs.unimal.ac.id/mjml/index
title: Use meta-analytic moderator results to help teachers choose student-centred strategies, methods, or techniques for primary school mathematics outcomes
description: The article positions its synthesis as a resource for practice: teachers selecting among student-centred strategies, methods, and techniques, and curriculum developers setting teaching principles, can use the pooled effect size and moderator results when choosing an approach for primary school mathematics. The authors state that "Teachers can adopt the results of this study as an important source to help them choose a strategy, method, or technique in a course that is appropriate for the outcomes". The moderator analysis identifying application approach as the only significant moderator is the key input for such choices.
requirements: Access to the effect-size and moderator-analysis results when selecting a strategy, method, or technique for primary mathematics outcomes
constraints: The research is limited by its inclusion criteria (studies from 2008-2018, experimental, primary school samples, non-longitudinal)
Only the application approach moderator showed a statistically significant difference between levels
target_learners: Primary school students in mathematics courses
target_learning_goals: Primary school mathematics academic achievement
examples: The meta-analysis compared nine application approaches (e.g., ABMI d = 1.334, Educational Games d = 1.280, PBL d = 0.356) to identify which student-centred approaches showed the largest effects

article_title: Methodology to the Teaching of English as a Foreign Language: A Systematic Review
citation: Philominraj, A., Ranjan, R., Ubilla Rosales, L., Cocio, A., & Brauchy Castillo, J. G. (2023). Methodology to the Teaching of English as a Foreign Language: A Systematic Review. MEXTESOL Journal, 47(2). https://www.mextesol.net/journal/
title: Chilean national English curriculum combines the Communicative Approach with Natural Approach, Cooperative Learning, Content-Based Instruction and Task-Based Language Teaching
description: The review describes the Chilean National Curriculum's English programs as anchored in the Communicative Approach and supplemented by four further approaches promoting communication. It states: "Themain contributions come from: a) Natural Approach; b) CooperativeLearning; c) Content-Based Instruction and d) Task-Based Language teaching". The curriculum emphasizes development of critical and creative thinking, teaching of learning strategies, communicative tasks, connections, culture, the writing process, and ICT and multimodal texts (MINEDUC, 2015), with class activities involving pair work, role play, problem solving and collaborative group projects.
requirements: Class objectives address all language components (vocabulary, topics, grammar, strategies, functions) across the four skills of listening, reading, writing, and speaking
constraints: The pattern is prescribed by the Chilean Ministry of Education curriculum, mandatory from fifth grade (students 10 years old)
target_learners: Chilean students aged 10–18 in mandatory English schooling, plus tertiary learners
target_learning_goals: Communicative competence: using English to interact and communicate relevant messages in contextualized, meaningful ways
examples: Under the communicative approach, work activities are developed in pairs, roleplay, problem-solving, and collaborative group projects in which students negotiate meanings and exchange information

article_title: Effectiveness of school-based CPR training among adolescents to enhance knowledge and skills in CPR: A systematic review.
citation: Zenani, N.E., Bello, B., Molekodi, M., & Useh, U., 2022, 'Effectiveness of school-based CPR training among adolescents to enhance knowledge and skills in CPR: A systematic review', Curationis 45(1), a2325. https://doi.org/10.4102/curationis.v45i1.2325
title: Chain of survival as the framework linking bystander CPR training to out-of-hospital cardiac arrest survival
description: The review frames school-based CPR training through the chain of survival: early recognition of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, activating the emergency response, early CPR with chest compressions, rapid defibrillation, and post-CPR care. Because these "critical linked interventions mostly rely on a layperson, who is often the first on the scene", training adolescents in school positions them to act promptly and to serve as CPR multipliers passing skills to family and friends.
requirements: Laypersons trained in the chain of survival links must be present at the scene of cardiac arrest
constraints: The framework is presented in the review's introduction as background rationale, not tested within the review itself
target_learners: adolescent schoolchildren
lay bystanders
target_learning_goals: recognising cardiac arrest
activating emergency response
performing early CPR with chest compressions
examples: The review describes a pupil trained in CPR saving another pupil on the soccer field when a teacher is absent, acting according to the chain of survival links

article_title: A systematic review and meta-analysis of online versus alternative methods for training licensed health care professionals to deliver clinical interventions.
citation: Richmond Helen, Copsey Bethan, Hall Amanda M., Davies David, Lamb Sarah E. (2017). A systematic review and meta-analysis of online versus alternative methods for training licensed health care professionals to deliver clinical interventions. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-017-1047-4
title: Choose between online and alternative training methods for licensed health professionals based on resources, expertise, and desired reach, since effectiveness for knowledge and clinical behaviour appears similar
description: The review's practical implication for educators: because online training may be as effective as alternative methods for providing knowledge and achieving desired clinical behaviour, the choice of method should be governed by contextual factors. The article states that "factors such as the availability of resources, expertise, and desired reach of an intervention may govern which training method is optimal in any given scenario." Online methods offer widespread access, personalised instruction, and regularly updated content, but face-to-face workshops remain the current gold standard.
requirements: A robust, direct comparison study is still needed before recommending online methods for practical skills, satisfaction, and self-efficacy
constraints: The low quality of the evidence precludes drawing firm conclusions on the relative effectiveness of these training methods
target_learners: Licensed health care professionals
target_learning_goals: Clinical intervention training outcomes of knowledge and clinical behaviour
examples: The review pooled 14 RCTs comparing online training with workshops, lectures, and manuals and found little difference on knowledge and clinical behaviour outcomes

A systematic review and meta-analysis of online versus alternative methods for training licensed health care professionals to deliver clinical interventions. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-017-1047-4

article_title: Which intervention design factors influence performance of community health workers in low- and middle-income countries? A systematic review.
citation: Kok Maryse C, Dieleman Marjolein, Taegtmeyer Miriam, Broerse Jacqueline EW, Kane Sumit S, Ormel Hermen, Tijm Mandy M, de Koning Korrie AM. (2014). Which intervention design factors influence performance of community health workers in low- and middle-income countries? A systematic review. Health Policy and Planning. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4597042/
title: Preliminary conceptual framework of factors influencing CHW performance with three outcome levels
description: The review developed a preliminary conceptual framework (Figure 1) dividing factors influencing CHW performance into three main categories: broad contextual factors, health system factors and intervention design factors. It differentiates "CHW performance outcome measures at three levels (Figure 1): CHW level, mediating processes and end-user level", with CHW-level outcomes including self-esteem, motivation, attitudes, competencies, adherence to standards and procedures, job satisfaction and capacity to facilitate community agency. The framework guided data extraction and categorization of findings, and new subcategories deriving from the literature were added where needed.
requirements: The framework was developed from reading selected international literature and used as the basis for data extraction and categorization of findings
constraints: This review limits itself to presenting intervention design factors; broad contextual and health system factors are presented in a separate article
target_learners: community health workers in low- and middle-income countries
target_learning_goals: CHW motivation, competencies, job satisfaction and adherence to standards and procedures
examples: The framework was used to structure the data extraction form and thematic coding of all 140 included studies

article_title: Effectiveness of problem-based learning in Chinese pharmacy education: a meta-analysis.
citation: Zhou Jiyin, Zhou Shiwen, Huang Chunji, Xu Rufu, Zhang Zuo, Zeng Shengya, Qian Guisheng. (2016). Effectiveness of problem-based learning in Chinese pharmacy education: a meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-016-0546-z
title: Corpus of 16 Chinese-language randomized controlled trials of PBL in pharmacy education (2006–2014, pooled n = 1826)
description: The meta-analysis assembles a corpus of 16 articles (representing 17 studies) published in Chinese between 2006 and 2014, previously inaccessible to non-Chinese-speaking researchers. "The sample sizes ranged from 28 to 112 participants and the pooled sample size was 1826 (PBL group = 929, control group = 897)". Studies spanned pharmacy disciplines including pharmaceutical analysis, natural medicine chemistry, biopharmaceutics and pharmacokinetics, pharmaceutical formulation design, and others, with intervention lengths of one to two semesters.
requirements: Chinese-language database access (CNKI, VIP, Wanfang, CBM) for retrieval
constraints: All studies were conducted in mainland China; none assessed long-term professional achievements of pharmacists
target_learners: Undergraduate pharmacy students in Chinese colleges and universities
target_learning_goals: Theoretical examination performance in pharmacy coursework
examples: The search identified 419 abstracts, of which 166 duplicates were removed and 56 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility before final inclusion of 16 studies
key_sources: Zhou Jiyin, Zhou Shiwen, Huang Chunji, Xu Rufu, Zhang Zuo, Zeng Shengya, Qian Guisheng. (2016). Effectiveness of problem-based learning in Chinese pharmacy education: a meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-016-0546-z

article_title: The Effects of 5E Inquiry Learning Activities on Achievement and Attitude toward Chemistry
citation: Senol Sen & Ozge Ozyalcin Oskay. (2016). The Effects of 5E Inquiry Learning Activities on Achievement and Attitude toward Chemistry. Journal of Education and Learning, 6(1). https://doi.org/10.5539/jel.v6n1p1
title: Chemical Equilibrium Concept Test (CECT)
description: The CECT is a researcher-developed instrument used to measure conceptual achievement in chemical equilibrium as pre-test and post-test. It consists of "16 multiple choice questions cont aining two stages" about factors influencing chemical equilibrium, with two-stage scoring in which a question earns credit only if both stages are answered correctly. Content validity was checked by two chemistry lecturers, and item discrimination and difficulty indices informed revisions.
requirements: Expert opinion from chemistry lecturers for content validity
reliability and item analyses during development
constraints: Cronbach Alpha internal coefficient was .73 for the 16-question test
target_learners: undergraduate chemistry students
target_learning_goals: conceptual achievement in chemical equilibrium
examples: Administered to both groups in the first week (pre-test) and final week (post-test) of the five-week study

article_title: TextNow Transition Programme: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Maxwell, B., Connolly, P., Demack, S., O'Hare, L., Stevens, A., & Clague, L. (2014). TextNow Transition Programme: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://www.educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk
title: The 'choose, enjoy and understand' rubric underlying the TextNow programme
description: TextNow coaching is organised around three strands captured by the rubric that the programme's "role of the coach is to support the three Text Now core principals of 'choose, enjoy and understand'". 'Choosing texts' develops pupils' skills in selecting suitable, interesting reading materials and familiarity with environments where texts are found; 'enjoying texts' uses shared reading, ICT, audio books and related discussion; 'understanding texts' targets literal and inferential comprehension through techniques such as skimming and scanning, KWL, storyboards and reciprocal teaching. The report situates this as a model with strong common-sense appeal but inconclusive causal evidence.
requirements: Coaches plan sessions from a reading profile created after a reading interview and increasingly focus on the young person's interests and needs
constraints: The report states there is a lack of systematic evidence in the wider academic literature for a pathway of causality between choice and comprehension, and at least one experimental study shows no link between pupil choice and engagement with reading
Attributes other than 'understand' are hard to define and measure reliably
target_learners: Struggling readers at the primary-secondary transition
target_learning_goals: Independent reading
Reading enjoyment and motivation
Reading comprehension at literal and inferential levels
examples: Coaching activities for the choosing strand include talking about book choice, developing strategies to assess a book choice, visiting a library and using MyChoice!
key_sources: Maxwell, B., Connolly, P., Demack, S., O'Hare, L., Stevens, A., & Clague, L. (2014). TextNow Transition Programme: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED581131

article_title: Research Learning Communities: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Dr Jo Rose, Professor Sally Thomas, Dr Lei Zhang, Dr Anna Edwards, Dr Andres Augero, Ms Pooneh Roney. (2017). Research Learning Communities: Evaluation report and executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://www.educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk
title: Sustain Evidence Champion continuity, time and resource access for research-use interventions to implement successfully
description: The process evaluation identified implementation conditions for research-use interventions: staff turnover, competing priorities and limited teacher time were barriers because Evidence Champions must commit for the full duration, attend all workshops, and have in-school time to develop ideas and discuss with colleagues. The report also notes "a lack of access to resources such as subscription journals may also limit the successful implementation of RLC activity by restricting the range and recentness of the evidence" teachers can draw on.
requirements: Evidence Champions need to be able to commit to the full duration of the intervention, attend all the workshops, and have time in school to develop their ideas and discuss the project with their colleagues
constraints: some schools did not allocate any extra dedicated time beyond the workshops
target_learners: primary school teachers acting as Evidence Champions
target_learning_goals: sustained school engagement with educational research
examples: In some schools different people were allocated the Champion role in Year 2, and some schools sent different people to different workshops

article_title: Should Peer E-Comments Replace Traditional Peer Comments?
citation: Ho, P. V. P., Phung, L. T. K., Oanh, T. T. T., & Giao, N. Q. (2020). Should Peer E-Comments Replace Traditional Peer Comments? International Journal of Instruction, 13(1), 295-314. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2020.13120a
title: Choose the peer-comment platform according to the teaching context's technology access and teacher comfort
description: The article recommends that neither mode universally replace the other: the decision "depends on the teachers’ professional contexts, available facilities, and teachers’ comfort of using technology." Where technology is supported, peer e-comments were the better choice in this study; where teachers or students are uncomfortable with technology, traditional paper-and-pen peer comments remain effective for improving writing quality. Teachers should weigh student access to the Internet and computers when selecting the platform.
requirements: peer commenting activities must be well designed and students trained in giving comments
constraints: paper-and-pen mode suits students without regular Internet access or computers; Facebook mode presumes technology access and teacher comfort
target_learners: EFL writing teachers and their university students
target_learning_goals: improving students' L2 writing quality through peer feedback
examples: The study's own teachers applied the same training procedures in both modes, differing only in the comment platform, and found both effective with Facebook more so

article_title: Chatterbooks: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Styles, B., Clarkson, R., & Fowler, K. (2014). Chatterbooks: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://www.educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk
title: Chatterbooks and Chatterbooks Plus reading-group programmes with the SPICE dialogic reading sequence
description: Chatterbooks is an extracurricular reading initiative by the Reading Agency aiming to "increase a child's motivation to read" through weekly small-group sessions where pupils read and discuss an age-appropriate book. Chatterbooks Plus replaces 15 minutes of each hour-long session with dialogic reading structured by the SPICE prompt sequence: Share a text, Prediction, Improve it, Cognitions, Emotions. In this trial both were delivered by trained graduates over nine weekly sessions to Year 7 pupils who had not reached a secure Level 4 in English.
requirements: A session run by a 'tutor' with good knowledge of children's literature and enthusiasm for reading
Adequate bookstock for children to choose texts from each week
A suitable 'non formal' location
constraints: Both variants evaluated were changed significantly from the established extracurricular Chatterbooks programme running since 2001
Chatterbooks Plus had not been trialled in any form before this evaluation
target_learners: Year 7 pupils who had not reached a secure Level 4 in English at the end of Key Stage 2
target_learning_goals: Reading ability
Motivation to read for pleasure
Reading comprehension skills
examples: Nine weekly one-hour sessions delivered in school libraries or empty classrooms, with playful activities such as craft activities, quizzes and role play
key_sources: Styles, B., Clarkson, R., & Fowler, K. (2014). Chatterbooks: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED581155

article_title: The Effects of Two Teachers' Instructional Methods on Students' Learning Outcomes in Chemistry in Selected Senior Secondary School in Kaduna Metropolis, Nigeria
citation: Efe M. Omwirhiren, Khalil U. Ibrahim. (2016). The Effects of Two Teachers' Instructional Methods on Students' Learning Outcomes in Chemistry in Selected Senior Secondary School in Kaduna Metropolis, Nigeria. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.15. https://www.iiste.org
title: Chemical Bonding Performance Test (CBPT)
description: The Chemical Bonding Performance Test (CBPT) was the instrument developed and validated for the study, consisting of twenty-five multiple choice test items adopted from WAEC past question papers for 2010-2015 chemistry examinations. It covers forces within molecules, the ionic bond, covalent bond, overlaps of atomic orbitals, bond polarity: dipoles, metallic bond and intermolecular forces. Its reliability coefficient, computed with SPSS from pilot data, was 0.654.
requirements: Content and face validity by scrutiny of specialists in chemistry and curriculum before administration
constraints: Reliability coefficient of 0.654 as computed from the pilot study sample of 45 SS II students
target_learners: Senior secondary (SS II) science students
target_learning_goals: Assessment of students' understanding of chemical bonding
examples: The CBPT was pilot tested with 45 SS II students at Government Technical College, Malali to establish item analysis, item difficulty, facility indices and reliability.

article_title: Chess in Schools: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: John Jerrim, Lindsey Macmillan, John Micklewright, Mary Sawtell and Meg Wiggins. (2016). Chess in Schools: Evaluation report and executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/library/chess-in-schools-protocol/
title: Chess in Primary Schools programme (CSC 30-hour curriculum intervention)
description: A whole-school approach in which Year 5 children receive 30 hours of chess lessons delivered during the school day by a trained chess tutor following a standardised CSC curriculum, with an optional lunchtime or after-school chess club. Lessons use whole-class teaching with a demonstration board or whiteboard software, and children share chess sets to practise moves and play games in pairs. The programme was delivered by the charity Chess in Schools and Communities at a cost of approximately £1,900 per school for two classes, or £32 per pupil.
requirements: A designated class teacher or teaching assistant attends a CSC training seminar and works with the tutor
Schools replace one regularly scheduled lesson (not maths or English) to make room for chess lessons
constraints: Tutors were chess specialists and did not necessarily have a teaching background
Some schools reduced the number of maths lessons in the timetable to accommodate chess lessons
target_learners: Year 5 primary school pupils (age 9/10) in England, in schools with high proportions of disadvantaged pupils
target_learning_goals: Concentration
strategic thinking
self-confidence
and ultimately academic achievement in mathematics
examples: In the trial, 100 schools delivered the programme across the 2013/2014 academic year, with tutors encouraged to talk for no more than 15 minutes before allowing children to practise

article_title: Validity of a Checklist for the Design, Content, and Instructional Qualities of Children's Books
citation: Erkan Çer, Ertuğrul Şahin. (2016). Validity of a Checklist for the Design, Content, and Instructional Qualities of Children's Books. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.24. https://www.iiste.org
title: Checklist of quality children's books (Çer & Şahin, 2016)
description: A measurement instrument for assessing children's books across three dimensions. The article states it "focuses on the assessment of children's books in terms of the design, con tent, and instructional qualities": instructional qualities cover advice and orders, teaching and memorising, fear and anxiety, gender discrimination, ideological discourse, traditional values, extremely emotional elements, and violence; design covers fonts, paper quality, dimensions, page layout, binding, and visuals; content covers plots, characters, messages, and use of language. In this study both groups learned to use the checklist and rated books with it.
requirements: Raters must be trained in how to use the checklist before rating books, as both groups in the study were
constraints: The article notes the checklist is time-consuming because of its length, and its validity has not been tested across children's age groups
target_learners: prospective Turkish language teachers (university students)
target_learning_goals: assessing the quality of children's books
examples: Experimental-group books included Balina ile Mandalina by Fazıl Hüsnü Dağlarca and My Name is Nobody by Frank Cottrell Boyce; control-group books included Falaka by Ahmet Rasim and Mutlu Prens by Oscar Wilde
key_sources: Erkan Çer, Ertuğrul Şahin. (2016). Validity of a Checklist for the Design, Content, and Instructional Qualities of Children's Books. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.24. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1112922

article_title: Validity of a Checklist for the Design, Content, and Instructional Qualities of Children's Books
citation: Erkan Çer, Ertuğrul Şahin. (2016). Validity of a Checklist for the Design, Content, and Instructional Qualities of Children's Books. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.24. https://www.iiste.org
title: Instructional-quality criteria pattern: what children's books should and should not contain
description: A reusable evaluation pattern specifying the instructional qualities a children's book should avoid and foster. The article states that "such elements as advice and orders, te aching and memorising, fear and anxiety, gender d iscrimination, ideological discourse, traditional values, rules and prescriptive judgments, singular and never-changing truths, extremely emotional experiences, and violence of a psychological, emotional, or physical nature should not exist in children's books." Instead, books should contain elements that let children imagine, think freely, make decisions, cope with violence, foster creativity, and use initiative without emotional exploitation.
requirements: Assessment must consider instructional qualities alongside design and content, since a book is not content alone
constraints: The article argues books should not be too protective and should help children face themes like death, sickness, divorce, and violence as part of life
target_learners: children at primary and secondary school levels
target_learning_goals: critical thinking
creativity
coping with difficult life themes
examples: The checklist's instructional-quality subscales operationalize this pattern, and Table 1 reports significantly higher ratings for quality books on each subscale

article_title: Applying Computer-Assisted Musical Instruction to Music Appreciation Course: An Example with Chinese Musical Instruments
citation: Lou, S.-J., Guo, Y.-C., Zhu, Y.-Z., Shih, R.-C., & Dzan, W.-Y. (2011). Applying computer-assisted musical instruction to music appreciation course: An example with Chinese musical instruments. The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 10(1). https://www.tojet.net/
title: Chinese Musical Instrument CAMI software
description: A Flash-based computer-assisted musical instruction package developed by the authors for the Learning Chinese Musical Instruments course. It "consists of six parts, including a brief introduction to Chinese musical instruments, the classification patterns of Chinese musical instruments, blowing and wind instruments, string instruments, psaltery instruments, and percussion instruments." Under each instrument type it provides introduction, structure, performance, tuning and compass, short story, and comparison, plus performance film clips and evaluation pages for matching instruments to names.

Requires computers, projection and audio equipment in specialized classrooms per the article's administrative recommendation
constraints: Did not include explanation of melody or introduction of instrumental ensembles, limited by manpower and funding
Designed primarily for teacher use, with limited student-software interaction

examples: Administered to 228 students over five weeks; the evaluation page "enables the teacher to assess if the learner fully understands the classifications of musical instruments"

article_title: An Analysis of the Effect of a Cyber Home Learning System on Korean Secondary School Students' English Language Achievement and Attitude
citation: Ji Hye Shin & Peggy Albers. (2015). An Analysis of the Effect of a Cyber Home Learning System on Korean Secondary School Students' English Language Achievement and Attitude. TESL Canada Journal/Revue TESL du Canada, 32(2). https://www.teslcanadajournal.ca
title: Cyber Home Learning System (CHLS) self-study option for Grade 9 English
description: The CHLS is a national open-access learning system implemented in South Korea in 2004 enabling K–12 learners with web access to study topics including English, created "to close the educational access divide, to reduce private tutoring expenses, and to improve the quality of public education." It offers a classroom option with cyber-teacher management and a self-study option where students select content by preference. In this study the self-study option comprised 12 units of 9 lessons each, with tasks structured as Motivation, Learning Instructions, Task 1–3, and Wrap-up, plus Need Help and Challenge buttons.
requirements: Students need web access; the experimental condition required daily self-study of at least one task, supported by course credits for regular login activity
constraints: Units include no pre-assessments; formal assessments occur only at the end of each unit
target_learners: Grade 9 secondary EFL students in South Korea
target_learning_goals: English language proficiency (listening, reading, writing)
examples: In the study, experimental-group students self-studied at home with CHLS for four weeks in addition to regular classroom instruction

article_title: Efficacy of the Check & Connect Mentoring Program for At-Risk General Education High School Students
citation: Heppen, J. B., Zeiser, K., Holtzman, D. J., O'Cummings, M., Christenson, S., & Pohl, A. (2017). Efficacy of the Check & Connect Mentoring Program for At-Risk General Education High School Students. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness. https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2017.1318990
title: Check & Connect theory of action: student engagement as the primary mediator linking mentoring to school completion
description: The article describes a theory of action in which trained mentors' persistent support improves students' behavioral, affective, and cognitive engagement, which improves interim academic outcomes (persistence, course performance, credit accrual, achievement) and ultimately on-time graduation. Engagement is described as "a primary mediator for promoting school completion" and as multidimensional, spanning behavioral, affective, and cognitive engagement. The framework draws on research on resiliency, systems theory, cognitive-behavioral theory, and intrinsic motivation, and is depicted in Figure 1 with some cyclical interrelationships.
requirements: Mentors systematically monitor attendance, social/behavior performance, and academic performance using school data (the check component) and build relationships through formal and informal meetings (the connect component)
constraints: The article notes the depicted process is shown as linear but some interrelationships among components may be cyclical
target_learners: General education high school students showing early warning signs of dropout risk (Grades K-12 per the program design)
target_learning_goals: School engagement
course performance and credit accrual
on-time high school graduation
examples: In the trial, mentors worked one-on-one with students for three years starting the summer after Grade 9, using check data and basic or intensive interventions aligned to the theory of action

article_title: Changing Mindsets: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Cinzia Rienzo, Heather Rolfe and David Wilkinson (NIESR). (2015). Changing Mindsets: Evaluation report and Executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk
title: Changing Mindsets pupil workshops intervention
description: A six-week course of mentoring and workshops for Year 5 pupils, delivered in schools by trained university students employed as project support assistants (PSAs), followed by four further weeks of sessions and visits delivered by the Education Business Partnership and Pompey Study Centre. The workshops "taught pupils about the malleable nature of intelligence, and sought to help pupils develop a growth mindset", including hands-on maths and literacy work demonstrating how not giving up and exploring different strategies helps find solutions. Workshops ran for two hours weekly with a 3/15 staff/pupil ratio.
requirements: PSAs recruited competitively and trained in mindset, behaviour management and workshop delivery by the University of Portsmouth academic team
constraints: The report notes the format of the course was standardised across schools only as far as possible
target_learners: Year 5 pupils in schools with low attainment
target_learning_goals: Growth mindset beliefs
Attainment in English and maths
examples: The intervention group received mindset workshops while the active control group received time-matched general study skills support, both delivered by PSAs.

article_title: Changing Mindsets: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Cinzia Rienzo, Heather Rolfe and David Wilkinson (NIESR). (2015). Changing Mindsets: Evaluation report and Executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk
title: Changing Mindsets teacher INSET intervention
description: A professional development course of two half-days of training in which University of Portsmouth staff trained teachers to teach pupils that intelligence is not fixed and to reinforce this through classroom communication. The first session introduced Dweck's mindset concept, US evidence of impact, and reconsidering whole-school and classroom culture regarding teacher expectation, use of language, reward systems and valuing learning from mistakes; the second, 6–8 weeks later, reviewed teachers' experiences and helped resolve challenges. The report notes it "was not therefore a manualised approach".
requirements: Teachers apply the general approach and specific techniques at their own discretion in teaching and learning
constraints: The report notes the intervention and control groups had different levels of FSM eligibility and prior attainment, risking compositional confounding
target_learners: Year 5 pupils taught by trained teachers
target_learning_goals: Teacher practices that encourage growth mindsets
Pupil attainment in English and maths
examples: Learning support staff were also invited to attend the training, and a number did so.

article_title: How Does Lesson Structure Shape Teacher Perceptions of Teaching with Challenging Tasks?
citation: James Russo, Sarah Hopkins. (2017). How does lesson structure shape teacher perceptions of teaching with challenging tasks? Mathematics Teacher Education and Development, 19(1), 30-46. https://www.merga.net.au
title: For teachers new to challenging tasks, incorporating cognitively demanding tasks in any capacity may be the more dramatic shift than the choice of lesson structure
description: The article concludes that for some teachers, particularly one who self-identified as having relatively limited mathematical content knowledge, the presence of challenging tasks may matter more than whether they launch or extend a lesson. As the authors put it, "the most dramatic shift in teaching practice for some teachers may be the incorporation of more cognitively demanding tasks into their mathematics instruction in any capacity". The article also suggests mastering challenging tasks to extend thinking may build skills for later task-first use.
requirements: Tasks must be designed as challenging (cognitively demanding) tasks with enabling and extending prompts, as used in the study's units
constraints: A teacher with self-identified limited content knowledge remained reluctant to use challenging tasks even in the Teach-First structure, so structure alone did not overcome reluctance
target_learners: early primary (Year 1/2) students
target_learning_goals: mathematics: number and algebra, problem solving with cognitively demanding tasks
examples: Three Year 1/2 classes experienced both structures across two units (Patterning, Addition) in a cross-over design, while their teachers observed and were interviewed; Polly, whose class used Teach-First first, still declined to teach with challenging tasks herself

article_title: High Quality Differentiated Instruction--A Checklist for Teacher Professional Development on Handling Differences in the General Education Classroom
citation: Wouter Smets. (2017). High Quality Differentiated Instruction – A Checklist for Teacher Professional Development on Handling Differences in the General Education Classroom. Universal Journal of Educational Research 5(11): 2074-2080. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2017.051124
title: Checklist for high quality differentiated instruction scaffolding teacher decision-making
description: A checklist that scaffolds teachers' professional decision-making with regard to differentiated instruction, developed through a systematic comparison of two expert DI models with three meta-analytic reference works on teaching effectivity. It consists of three sets of criteria covering the teacher-student relationship, learning goals, and lesson design. The authors state it "may aid teachers to assess and improve their own teaching practice" and is intended for personal or collective reflection by in-service teams and teacher students.
requirements: Teachers use it as a scaffold for reflective practice, not as a fixed to-do list; the article states items "are no fixed do's or don't"
constraints: The checklist was developed in Flanders, Belgium, based on two specific DI models and three generalist effectivity reference works
target_learners: pre-service and in-service general education teachers
target_learning_goals: evidence-informed decision-making when responding to student heterogeneity in the classroom
examples: A teacher uses the checklist in a staff meeting to question a school's homogeneous ability-group setting policy for mathematics

article_title: Overcoming the Research-to-Practice Gap: A Randomized Trial with Two Brief Homework and Organization Interventions for Students with ADHD as Implemented by School Mental Health Providers
citation: Langberg, J. M., Dvorsky, M. R., Molitor, S. J., Bourchtein, E., Eddy, L. D., Smith, Z. R., Oddo, L. E., & Eadeh, H.-M. (2017). title: CHIEF intervention: a 16-session brief school-based behavioral homework intervention
description: CHIEF (Completing Homework by Improving Efficiency and Focus) uses the same service delivery model as HOPS but targets the behavioral aspects of homework completion. During each of 16 meetings the provider "implements a behavior management and points system, sets work completion goals, and has the student complete homework and study for tests," token-rewarding on-task behavior and providing verbal praise. Two parent meetings teach caregivers to set work completion goals and run the point system at home; adherence averaged 89.23% of criteria met.
requirements: 16 meetings with the same service delivery model as HOPS
an operationalized work completion goal at the start of each meeting
a token system rewarding on-task behavior and two parent meetings
constraints: this was its first empirical evaluation; it does not teach organization and planning skills
target_learners: middle school students with ADHD
target_learning_goals: focus and efficiency during homework completion
on-task behavior
examples: Providers put a token in a jar for each minute the student remained on-task and were to give 10 verbal praises per meeting

article_title: Instructional Experiment of Practical Competencies-Oriented Teaching Materials in Technical Universities
citation: Su-Chang Chen, National Penghu University of Science and Technology, Taiwan. (2010). Instructional Experiment Of Practical Competencies-Oriented Teaching Materials In Technical Universities. American Journal of Business Education – September 2010 Volume 3, Number 9. https://clutejournals.com
title: Chen (2005) practical competencies-oriented teaching materials and local cases for business programs
description: A set of business-program teaching materials developed by Chen (2005) from practical competencies identified for technical-university graduates. The former study "invited 30 experienced supervisors and personnel from the business circle to participate in three Delphi questionnaire surveys", yielding "the 70 professional and practical competencies needed by graduates of the business program", which "had transformed the competencies into 15 courses". In this study the human resource management unit's materials and local cases were taught to the experimental group for three weeks.

title: Cultural-historical activity theory as a framework connecting group interactions to learning outcomes
description: The article uses second-generation cultural-historical activity theory (CHAT), which "considers how the relationships among people (the subjects), the activity (the object), tools, rules, community, and division of labor can all affect the final outcome." Because these connections are not always easily observable, the authors developed the graph theory methodology to quantify the division of labor, interactions among students and peer facilitators, and potentially hidden rules guiding engagement. constraints: Connections defined across the different components in CHAT cannot necessarily be easily seen directly

examples: Seating arrangements are treated as the tools component of CHAT, with circular seating associated with higher graph density than traditional front-facing seating
